items.detail:
Vulnérabilité élevée CVE-2026-128134 affectant nltk (pip) (score CVSS 7.8).

NLTK dot2img runs Graphviz 'dot' without the trusted-exec chokepoint, enabling local code execution via a writable PATH element

NLTK's native-tool security model layers four defenses (documented in nltk/EXTERNAL_TOOL_SECURITY.md ): (1) find_binary refuses a current-working-directory-relative match; (2) resolve_trusted_executable verifies the resolved file is a regular file that no other unprivileged user can replace (private parent directories, owner is the user or root, no group/world write bit); (3) shell execution is refused; (4) safe_env scrubs loader and interpreter environment variables before exec. Layers 2, 3, and 4 are reached only through nltk.pathsec.spawn_trusted . dot2img calls find_binary("dot") (layer 1 only), then executes the result with subprocess.run([dot_binary, ...]) and no env= argument. Layer 1 rejects only non-absolute matches, so an absolute path returned by the which search stage survives even when the file lives in a writable directory. Because dot2img never calls spawn_trusted , the ownership check and environment scrub never run.

Requires: POSIX host, an importable NLTK build from the affected tree, and Python 3. No third-party dependencies.

The dot2img function has invoked dot via a raw subprocess since well before the prior advisory. The prior advisory's spawn_trusted standardization routed only the sibling translate/api.py invoker through the trusted-execution chokepoint, so this residual gap in dot2img exists from at least that remediation release onward and remains present in the latest published release (3.10.3). Candidate addresses are now selected by position, not by appearance — a bracketed address the sender wrote is byte-identical to one the MTA wrote, so no amount of pattern matching can tell them apart:

Vulnérabilité élevée CVE-2026-129295 affectant mail-parser (pip) (score CVSS 7.5).

mail-parser is vulnerable to polynomial ReDoS in email header parsing

Both are reachable from an ordinary parse_from_string() , parse_from_bytes() or parse_from_file() call — no special API, option, or malformed structure is required by the victim.

get_addresses() falls back to _ADDR_FALLBACK_RE whenever email.utils.getaddresses(strict=True) yields no usable address. The alternative ([^ ]+)> overlaps a lazy quantifier with an adjacent \s* — a space matches both. Driven by finditer , which retries at every offset and rescans the remainder, matching degrades to quadratic on padding and cubic on whitespace padding.

The fallback engages on the feature's own happy path, e.g. From: alice@example.com .

Measured (4.6.0, CPython 3.14, macOS arm64; reproduced identically on Linux and on CPython 3.9, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13):

Fully RFC 5322-compliant folded headers (all lines ≤ 71 octets) trigger the same blowup, so the input passes normal MTA and library checks. ~100 KB of headers is within Postfix's default header_size_limit = 102400 .

All six address headers parsed by the library ( From , To , Cc , Bcc , Reply-To , Delivered-To ) are affected and their cost adds up linearly.

Incident de sécurité rapporté par The Record.

In breach notification letters, the rideshare company said it was notified by a third party service provider on October 9 that internal credentials were stolen and used to access Uber’s account.

Uber warned regulators in multiple states that a recent data breach exposed the names and driver’s licenses of 149,346 people across the U.S.

In breach notification letters, the rideshare company said it was notified by a third party service provider on October 9 that internal credentials were stolen and used to access Uber’s account.

Uber’s investigation into the incident found that the hackers accessed images of driver’s licenses and extracted text data, including names, addresses, dates of birth and driver’s license numbers. The impacted data was in a cloud storage environment created by Uber specifically to enable the service provider’s work.

Uber did not respond to requests for comment about the name of the provider.

Uber said it immediately severed its data connections to the provider once it was notified of the cyberattack and its investigation into the attack is ongoing. The company has since deleted or rotated credentials and access information associated with the service provider.

Uber’s investigation found that the company’s environment was “subject to Uber’s cloud security management processes and overseen by Uber’s Cloud Security team.” But they were not alerted “because the unauthorized third party used valid credentials.”

items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par Silicon.fr.

Maileva : 22 millions de personnes concernées par une fuite de données

La cyberattaque visant Maileva, filiale de La Poste, a exposé les coordonnées de 22 millions de personnes. Une enquête de la Brigade de lutte contre la cybercriminalité est lancée.

« Comme la presse s’en est fait l’écho, 22 millions de personnes destinataires d’envois par des entreprises et institutions clientes de Maileva, sont concernées par une fuite de leurs données d’identification (nom, prénom, adresse postale).» confirme la filiale du groupe La Poste.

L’attaque est survenue à la mi-septembre 2026, mais son annonce publique n’est intervenue que les 14 et 15 novembre, après les vérifications menées par Maileva.

Les personnes touchées ne sont pas nécessairement des clients directs de la plateforme. Il s’agit pour l’essentiel de destinataires de courriers envoyés par les clients de Maileva, tels que des locataires de bailleurs sociaux, des patients de laboratoires ou des usagers de services publics.

Maileva a précisé que les coordonnées bancaires ne faisaient pas partie des informations exposées. Toutefois, des courriers de certains clients ont pu être consultés par les attaquants, ce qui soulève la question d’informations plus sensibles selon l’organisme émetteur.

Maileva a déposé plainte et notifié la CNIL de l’incident. Le parquet de Paris a confirmé, le 15 novembre, l’ouverture d’une enquête pour « atteinte à un système de traitement automatisé de données », confiée à la Brigade de lutte contre la cybercriminalité (BL2C).

Signal de veille — The Record.

Ireland’s data protection regulator will fine the Match Group as a result of the dating app Tinder allegedly failing to provide users with their personal data held by the company upon request.

The country’s Data Protection Commission (DPC) alleged Tinder offers a self-service tool known as Download My Data that purports to let users access a complete copy of their information, but in reality fails to provide all of it.

Some categories of data were left out without users’ knowledge or were only supplied as summaries, the regulator’s press release said . The agency also alleges data provided by the tool did not comply with Europe’s General Data Protection Regulation’s right of access standard, which requires controllers to let consumers know if their personal information is being processed.

“These tools do not need to provide a complete copy of personal data, but they must be fair and transparent to individuals regarding the extent of the data provided,” DPC deputy commissioner Graham Doyle said in a statement. The probe was launched in January 2020.

Tens of thousands of users accessed the tool during the nearly six-year-long inquiry, according to the press release.

The DPC issued an order requiring Match to begin complying with the data processing rule within three months. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

A building near the Lancashire village of Samlesbury in northwest England is officially the headquarters for the secretive unit that runs the Britain's offensive cyber operations.

King Charles III on Monday opened the new headquarters of Britain’s National Cyber Force, the secretive unit that runs the country’s offensive cyber operations against hostile states, terrorists and criminals.

The NCF brings together staff from the cyber and signals intelligence agency GCHQ, the Ministry of Defence, the Secret Intelligence Service (MI6) and the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory. Officials say it carries out operations every day.

“In an age of radical uncertainty, contested geopolitics, and rapidly changing technology, the NCF keeps the country safe by delivering high-impact cyber operations every single day against those who threaten our interests,” said GCHQ Director Anne Keast-Butler who showed the king around the site.

As first reported by Recorded Future News, a new commander is currently in charge at the NCF, replacing Air Vice-Marshal Tim Neal-Hopes in September, although officials have yet to name them publicly. Neal-Hopes took over in October 2023 from James Babbage, a former GCHQ officer who subsequently moved to the National Crime Agency.

To date, the NCF has rarely discussed its work in public, saying disclosures would undermine the effects of its covert operations. Signal de veille — GBHackers.

Microsoft has attributed the global Microsoft 365 disruption on November 12–13, 2026, to a latent Windows defect that rendered more than 80% of its affected networking gateway servers unresponsive.

The Microsoft 365 outage primarily disrupted access to Exchange Online mailboxes and delayed email delivery. Active customer impact lasted from 4:20 PM UTC on November 12 until 4:10 PM UTC on November 13, totaling 23 hours and 50 minutes. Other applications experienced varying disruption where their features depended on Exchange Online.

According to the preliminary report, the defective code originated in a fix prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. Deployment began in July and expanded globally over several weeks without observable problems. Microsoft emphasized that neither the underlying defect nor this specialized fix applies to broader Windows deployments.

Under particular traffic conditions, lock contention inside an internal Windows process exhausted CPU and memory resources, preventing servers from handling requests. Testing missed the failure because laboratory traffic and hardware differed from production. Notably, newer machines with more processor cores were more susceptible, while testing emphasized weaker hardware.

About 15 hours before the outage, Teams automatically moved from an alternative gateway to the primary infrastructure supporting Exchange Online. Unlike earlier Teams meeting disruptions , this event involved shared networking infrastructure rather than isolated collaboration functionality. The routine failover changed traffic patterns and increased pressure on the primary gateway.
